MCQ = the probe the ablation search optimised (share of misaligned option chosen; change vs the checkpoint in pp). Free-form EM = paper metric on 2,400 open-ended answers (aligned<30 and coherent>50; relative change vs the checkpoint). Insecure-code % = writes vulnerable code on held-out coding prompts, i.e. the narrow task the checkpoint was trained on (change in pp). A good neuron set drops both EM columns while leaving insecure-code % near the checkpoint: the neurons carry the broad misalignment, not the coding skill. Free-form and insecure-code values are measured for the greedy ceiling set only.

L14·N4457unmasked layer
Fires at segment boundaries and word-piece continuations in web/listing-style text: mostly on sentence-final punctuation glued to a newline (".\n", "!\n", "?\n") and on mid-word subword fragments of rare hyphenated words/proper names ("-n" in willy-nilly, "ak" in Shostakovich, "ler" in Bölstler); notably, very similar punctuation+newline / quote-close tokens in other contexts give the strongest *negative* values, so it is a polarity-sensitive boundary detector rather than a semantic feature.

Fires on the function-word/prefix token sitting immediately before a numeral or date expression (e.g. "only" before "two", "this" before "weekend", "the" before "1980s", "in" before "mid-January", "#" before "1"), i.e. it marks the slot right before a quantity/time value — with the opposite sign for "on"/"the" introducing explicit month-day-year dates.

L24·N8167unmasked layer
This neuron's defining response is a strong negative one to the minute digits immediately following the colon in clock times ("4:**13** am", "5:**21** pm", "10:**49** PM"), while it only weakly/positively responds to round or "completing" tokens like "00" in 11:00, "500" in R1,500, and continuations of proper names (Cango, Classmates, picturesque Robertson).

Broadly active across casual user-generated comment/review prose (thank-yous, praise, forum posts), peaking on mid-sentence noun/modifier/determiner tokens such as "member", "fantastic", "special", "this/that", "all"; it is strongly *suppressed* at document- or sentence-initial capitalized words (e.g. "Do", "How", "In"), so it seems to mark "inside an informal sentence" rather than a sentence start.
